continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: DevOps is one of those terms that means a lot of things to different people. You helped write the book on Continuous Delivery, which helped lead into kind of what we call DevOps. Can you tell us a little bit about what that means to you and how that relates to your talk today?
continuous-delivery.video: Jez Humble on DevOps Culture and Practices | GOTO Conference 2014

continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: Yeah, and you know, even outside that cycle, I mean, the point of continuous delivery is to give you this capability to be able to get changes out fast to users in a low risk way and to make it economic to work in small batches. But once you have that capability, the question then becomes, what do you do with it? And, you know, that I think, you know, the people in the DevOps field will tell you that you use that for creating a feedback loop so that you can make sure that you're working on the right things, so that you're building things that actually delight users and improve the customer experience. And so it kind of feeds into that whole discussion around making building things that are delightful and better serve our customers. And is that what your goal of your talk was?
continuous-delivery.video: Jez Humble on DevOps Culture and Practices | GOTO Conference 2014

continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: The book is called Lean Enterprise. And the book is about how large companies can innovate at scale. The problem that we have with the Continuous Delivery book is we talk about technical practices and principles, but organizations have trouble implementing them due to architecture, governance, compliance, or budgeting. Big companies that don't treat IT as a competitive advantage treat software as an order-taking cost center. Imagine if software actually was a competitive advantage to your business—Netflix and Google treat software as central to product development and innovation.
continuous-delivery.video: Jez Humble on DevOps Culture and Practices | GOTO Conference 2014

continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: Yeah, it's a huge problem—even understanding the concepts, the names, and how they fit together. People make basic mistakes with this stuff. It's genuinely counterintuitive. A lot of people think lean is about cutting costs. Lean is not about cutting costs; lean is about reducing waste. By reducing waste, we end up with lower costs, but you don't just look for expensive things and cut them out of the budget. Look at Toyota—Japanese culture had jobs for life, so you couldn't fire anyone. The idea with lean was to increase productivity by making people more efficient and effective, freeing up people to work on higher-value growth instead of firing them.
continuous-delivery.video: Jez Humble on DevOps Culture and Practices | GOTO Conference 2014

continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: All the time! People expect me to be a continuous delivery guy talking about technical things. But the problem is leadership and culture, so I tend to talk about those things these days. The most I can hope is that people come away with a bunch of ideas they can try out. They didn't get what they asked for, but they got what they needed!
continuous-delivery.video: Jez Humble on DevOps Culture and Practices | GOTO Conference 2014

continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: The main idea behind lean is to optimize the entire system, not just a specific part of it. It involves thinking about the whole and the high-level objectives of what you're doing.

continuous-delivery.speaker: Jez Humble
continuous-delivery.text: Lean thinking helps in creating empathy by understanding the needs and objectives of all the different people involved. It encourages thinking about how all these different parts fit together to create a bigger picture.

tdd-and-testing.text: NetBSD has a unique culture of testing that is not typically possible in a kernel. They have special technology in the kernel called 'Any Kernel,' which allows any component of the kernel to be targeted either for direct linking into a monolithic kernel or compiling it into a thin layer on top of some other system or into a standalone program with all the source code in it. This means you can write automated tests for kernel code that, when they break, don't mean your system crashed; it just means your process crashed, and your test harness can keep running, record the failure, and provide fast feedback. This is not only about security but also about testability.

tdd-and-testing.speaker: Amitai Schlair
tdd-and-testing.text: This approach to testing benefits NetBSD users by providing fast feedback and the ability to identify and fix issues more quickly. tdd-and-testing.text: I'm not really a fan of 100% code coverage, but some people are. That's gonna be a motivator for some of your tests. If you're not 100% code coverage, then you probably don't need to, say, test the methods of a framework that you're using.
tdd-and-testing.video: Unselfish Testing Practices: Mike Hall Interviews Jay Fields | GOTO Conference 2015

tdd-and-testing.speaker: Jay Fields
tdd-and-testing.text: So, know your motivators. I mean, the motivator of customer acceptance is another common one. Your manager told you to is another common one. There are a lot of reasons that people write tests, so the first thing, just know what direction your motivators are even putting you in. So, let's say that you only care about TDD for design, and another way that I like to look at my tests is RR. R-O-I, return on investment, and so, say, you only care about TDD, and you only care about ROI. So, cool. TDD everything. Get the benefits of TDD and get your improved design, you know, everything that everybody's been talking about with TDD. Do that. But just 'cause you wrote a test doesn't mean that it has to stay there.
tdd-and-testing.video: Unselfish Testing Practices: Mike Hall Interviews Jay Fields | GOTO Conference 2015

tdd-and-testing.speaker: Jay Fields
tdd-and-testing.text: It doesn't need to live there. Instead, I look at my tests, I prefer to look at my tests through ROI, and so every test has an ROI, negative or positive. And so, say you write a test, say you're an insurance company, and you need to look your customers up. Buy social security number. So, social needs to be correct, so you have a validation on social, but you don't need to get correct that they have no integers in their name, because there's no business value in keeping integers out of a name other than maybe, you know, one in a hundred, one in a million. You get a customer who's annoyed 'cause you put an integer in there, but they're not gonna cancel their insurance 'cause you put an integer in their name, right?
tdd-and-testing.video: Unselfish Testing Practices: Mike Hall Interviews Jay Fields | GOTO Conference 2015

tdd-and-testing.speaker: Jay Fields
tdd-and-testing.text: So, you don't necessarily need a test for that, but maybe you still TDD the feature, verifying that there's no integers in the name, you TDD it, and you get the good design benefits, delete the test, because if that gets broken, if there is a regression, it's minimal impact to the business.

tdd-and-testing.text: Actually, you brought up the next question I was gonna ask about culling tests, and that a lot of teams I've seen will take a test and treat it like it's a sync or synced thing that can never be, like, once it's implemented, you can't touch it, and just sometimes I look at tests and I'm like, "Why are we even testing this?
